title: Sikkim's organic farming story and what it means for you
meta_description: Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016 and won a 2018 Future Policy Gold Award. What that means on your plate, at markets and in homestays.
summary: Sikkim set out in 2003 to farm without chemical fertilisers and pesticides, and was declared India's first fully organic state at Gangtok in January 2016. In 2018 it won the Gold Future Policy Award. For travellers it means organic village food, Sunday markets and farm homestays, though not every plate in Gangtok is organic.

sections.heading: What fully organic actually means
paras: In Sikkim, organic is not a label on a fancy café menu. It is state policy. All of the state's farmland is certified organic, chemical fertilisers and pesticides have been phased out, and the sale and use of chemical pesticides is banned across the state. A farmer in Rhenock or Rumtek grows maize, ginger, cardamom and vegetables with compost, cow dung, green manure and traditional pest control, as many hill families did before fertiliser bags reached the mountains.

The policy covers farming, not everything that is eaten. Sikkim is small, steep and does not grow all the rice, dal, flour, oil and packaged food its people and visitors consume. Much of that still comes up NH10 from the plains. So when you eat in Gangtok, the greens, chhurpi, potatoes and pickles may well be from Sikkimese organic farms, while the rice and the biscuits probably are not. We tell guests this plainly because it is the honest version, and because the real organic food here is worth looking for.

sections.heading: How Sikkim got there
paras: The decision dates from 2003, when the state government set the goal of converting all farming to organic production. Over the next twelve years chemical fertilisers and pesticides were phased out, and farmers were trained in composting and organic methods, with their land brought under certification. In January 2016, at a gathering in Gangtok, Prime Minister Narendra Modi declared Sikkim India's first fully organic state.

International recognition followed. On 15 October 2018, at a ceremony at the headquarters of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization in Rome, Sikkim received the Gold Future Policy Award, given by the World Future Council with FAO and IFOAM – Organics International for the world's best policies on agroecology. The award noted that the change benefited more than 66,000 farming families, and that tourist numbers in Sikkim rose by more than 50 per cent between 2014 and 2017.

Agriculture remains a large employer in Sikkim, built on terraced fields of rice, maize, millet and cardamom, with oranges and tea in the warmer south. That is why the policy matters to so many households, and why it shows up so clearly in the villages you drive through.

sections.heading: What grows in East Sikkim
paras: East Sikkim's farms climb from warm river valleys at under 1,000 m to cold villages above 2,000 m, so what you see depends on where and when you go. Large cardamom is the region's best-known cash crop, and Sikkim grows more of it than any other Indian state. Ginger and turmeric grow on lower slopes, maize and millet on dry terraces, and rice in the wetter valleys. Higher up you find potatoes, buckwheat and cabbage.
The table below is a rough guide to what you might see on a drive or a village walk. Seasons shift by altitude and year.

Much of what grows here ends up fermented, dried or smoked, because hill families have always had to store food through the monsoon and winter. Gundruk is made from mustard, radish and cauliflower leaves wilted, packed tight and left to ferment for about a week, then sun-dried. Kinema is fermented soybean, a Limbu food now made across the Sikkim hills. Chhurpi starts as buttermilk from the family cow, boiled and drained into a soft cheese, and some of it is pressed and smoked until it is hard enough to chew slowly for a long time. All three are worth tasting at a homestay.

sections.heading: Where travellers can see it
paras: You do not need a special tour to see Sikkim's organic farming. You need to get out of the car. Every village homestay we use has a kitchen garden, and most families keep a cow or two for milk, chhurpi and manure. Ask your host to show you the compost pit, the seed store and the fields; most are glad to.

In Gangtok, the best place to see the produce is Lal Bazaar, the town's main market below MG Marg. On Sundays, village sellers come in for the haat and lay out mustard greens, watercress, fern shoots in season, chhurpi, dried fish and festive breads. For things to take home, the shops on and around MG Marg sell cardamom, ginger, turmeric, buckwheat flour and Sikkim tea from the Temi estate in the south.
list: Aritar and Rhenock: village homestays among terraces and cardamom groves, about 3 hours from Gangtok.
Rumtek and Ranka: farm villages within an hour of Gangtok; easy half-day walks between monasteries and fields.
Zuluk: high-altitude homestays where families still grow potatoes and greens at 2,900 m; Indian citizens only, with a permit.
Lal Bazaar, Gangtok: the Sunday haat for local produce and chhurpi.
Pakyong and Rorathang side: terraced farms visible from the alternative road to Siliguri.

sections.heading: Staying on a farm: what to expect
paras: A village homestay in East Sikkim usually costs ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with all meals, indicative 2026. The food is the point. Expect rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable from the garden, gundruk or a fermented pickle, and often chicken or pork. Breakfast may be sel roti or puri with potato curry and tea.

Rooms are simple and clean, with hot water by geyser or bucket. Electricity can fail in storms, and mobile signal is patchy. Families eat early, often by 8 pm, and the day starts at first light with the cows.

A few manners help. Take off your shoes inside the house. Ask before you walk through fields, and stay on the bunds rather than the planted soil. Do not pick fruit or cardamom pods unless invited. If you want to help with farm work, say so; many hosts will find you a job, from husking maize to carrying fodder. And please carry out any packaging you bring in; villages here manage their own waste.

sections.heading: Shopping and eating the organic way
paras: Some simple choices let you support Sikkim's farmers directly and eat better at the same time.
list: Order local vegetables, saag and gundruk in Gangtok's small eateries rather than paneer and plains dishes.
Buy cardamom, ginger and turmeric as whole spices; they keep well and pack small.
Try buckwheat pancakes or bread where you see them; buckwheat is a traditional high-hill crop.
Look for Temi tea, from Sikkim's own tea estate, instead of packaged brands.
At Lal Bazaar, buy from the village sellers on the floor rather than the wholesale stalls.
Carry a cloth bag; Sikkim discourages plastic, and sellers appreciate it.
Do not carry chemical sprays, fertiliser or plant material into village fields.

sections.heading: Limits and honest questions
paras: Sikkim's model is admired worldwide, but it is not a finished story, and you will meet people with different views. Farming is hard on these slopes, young people leave villages for jobs in Gangtok and beyond, and the state still depends on food from outside. Tourism, including homestays, has become one of the ways farm families earn a cash income alongside their crops.

Climate adds pressure. Landslides cut roads that carry produce to market, and a bad monsoon can wipe out a terrace in a night. Farmers along the Teesta side lost fields and access roads in the October 2023 flash flood. When you hear a host talk about a hard year, it is often the weather, not the farming method, that is to blame.

As a visitor, the most useful thing you can do is pay fairly for village stays and local food, and ask questions rather than assume. Ask your host how the change after 2003 affected their family. The answers vary from farm to farm, and that is the real story.

faqs.q: Is Sikkim really 100 per cent organic
faqs.a: Its farming is. All of Sikkim's farmland is certified organic, chemical fertilisers and pesticides have been phased out, and the sale and use of chemical pesticides is banned. Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in January 2016. But Sikkim does not grow all its own food, so rice, dal and packaged goods brought from the plains are not necessarily organic.

faqs.q: When did Sikkim become an organic state
faqs.a: Sikkim set the goal in 2003 and was declared India's first fully organic state in January 2016, at a gathering in Gangtok addressed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Over the years between, the state phased out chemical fertilisers and pesticides, trained farmers in organic methods and brought farmland under certification. In 2018 it won the Gold Future Policy Award.

faqs.q: What award did Sikkim win for organic farming
faqs.a: The Gold Future Policy Award 2018, presented on 15 October 2018 at the Food and Agriculture Organization's headquarters in Rome. The award is given by the World Future Council with FAO and IFOAM – Organics International. It recognised Sikkim's organic policy as one of the world's best for agroecology and sustainable food, noting benefits to more than 66,000 farming families.

faqs.q: Is food in Gangtok restaurants organic
faqs.a: Partly. Local greens, potatoes, chhurpi, pickles and fermented foods are likely to come from Sikkimese organic farms. Rice, flour, dal, cooking oil and packaged foods often come from the plains and may not be organic. For the most local plate, order seasonal saag, gundruk, chhurpi dishes and a homestyle thali in small eateries rather than plains dishes.

faqs.q: Where can I buy organic produce in Gangtok
faqs.a: Lal Bazaar, below MG Marg, is the best place, especially at the Sunday haat when village sellers bring greens, fern shoots, chhurpi and dried fish. Shops on and around MG Marg sell cardamom, ginger, turmeric, buckwheat flour and Temi tea that pack well for the journey home. Carry a cloth bag, since Sikkim discourages plastic.

faqs.q: Can I stay on an organic farm in East Sikkim
faqs.a: Yes. Registered village homestays around Aritar, Rhenock, Rumtek, Ranka and, for Indian citizens with a permit, Zuluk are working farm households. Expect ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals, indicative 2026, simple rooms and food from the family's own garden. Ask your host to show you the compost, seed store and fields; most are happy to.

faqs.q: What is the best season to see Sikkim's farms
faqs.a: October and November are our pick: rice harvest in the lower valleys, cardamom harvest ending, clear skies and dry paths. March and April bring spring sowing and flowering trees. Monsoon, from June to September, shows the terraces at their greenest, but paths are muddy and leeches are common in lower forests. Mandarin oranges ripen from November to January.

faqs.q: Can I bring fruit or plants into Sikkim
faqs.a: Carrying fruit to eat on the journey is normal. Avoid bringing seeds, saplings, chemical fertiliser or pesticide sprays into Sikkim, since the state bans chemical pesticides and protects its organic certification. If you are unsure about any item, leave it at home. Buy local produce once you arrive instead; it supports farmers and is fresher.

faqs.q: What spices should I buy in Sikkim
faqs.a: Large cardamom is the classic: Sikkim grows more of it than any other Indian state. Ginger, turmeric and dried local chillies are also good buys. Buy whole spices rather than powders; they keep longer and are harder to adulterate. Expect fair, fixed prices in MG Marg shops and lower prices from village sellers at Lal Bazaar's Sunday haat.
